message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, no mold, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or repair‑and‑deduct (but only after giving notice). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice if you’re unsure. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to privacy in your rented unit. Landlord cannot enter without notice or a valid reason. | • If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory actions to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the term ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the court process: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or a **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days) for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, seek legal help immediately. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to repair a problem and deduct the cost from rent **only** if the landlord fails to fix it after notice. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Rent increases must be in accordance with the lease or a new lease agreement. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Generally allowed if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you may want it for personal property protection. | • Consider a short‑term renters policy. | | **Legal Resources** | • **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** (https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection).
• **Texas Tenants’ Rights** (https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/tenants-rights).
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). | • Use these resources for disputes or to file complaints. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that the landlord will handle repairs and pest control. 3. **Confirm utility responsibilities** – who pays what? 4. **Check for “no‑cancellation” clauses** – some leases require a fee if you break early. 5. **Get everything in writing** – verbal agreements are hard to enforce. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Send a written notice (email/letter) and keep a copy | If no response in 10–14 days, consider repair‑and‑deduct or file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General | | Unlawful eviction notice | Verify the notice meets legal requirements (10‑day notice, proper reason) | Seek legal aid or contact a tenant‑rights group | | Discrimination | Document the incident | File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, reasonable notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for rent payment and lease termination. Keep written records, communicate in writing, and use the state’s consumer‑protection resources if you encounter problems.
